headline: A 20-minute workout or a nap helps a sleepless brain

sources.title: Workout or nap: either can help your sleepless brain, study finds
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

chunks.text: A night without sleep leaves memory weak and attention [[drifting]]. A new study from McGill University offers two ways to {{make up for}} the lost hours. A 20-minute [[workout]] or a 90-minute nap both helped tired brains remember images. Fifty-four healthy young adults {{took part}} in the experiment. They {{stayed up}} for 30 hours [[straight]], [[supervised]] by researchers in a [[laboratory]]. The results were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on September 8, 2026.

verbs.correct: To replace something that was lost
verbs.why: A worker can make up for a missed day by staying late, and a gift can make up for a forgotten birthday. The study found that a workout or a nap can make up for some of the memory lost after a sleepless night.

verbs.correct: To join an activity with others
verbs.why: Thousands of runners take part in the city marathon, and every student took part in the school play. Fifty-four healthy young adults took part in the McGill experiment.

verbs.correct: To remain awake instead of sleeping
verbs.wrong: To remain at home in the evening
verbs.why: Teenagers often stay up late playing video games, and parents stay up when a baby is sick. The volunteers stayed up for 30 hours straight in a laboratory.

chunks.text: After the long night, the [[volunteers]] were {{split up}} into three groups. One group cycled at [[moderate to vigorous]] effort for 20 minutes. A second group took a 90-minute nap. The third group did neither. Right after, everyone tried to {{take in}} a set of images. Three days later, the researchers tested how well those memories had {{held up}}. The exercise and nap groups both scored about 22 percent better than the group that did nothing.

verbs.correct: To divide people into smaller groups
verbs.wrong: To put your name on a list to join
verbs.why: The teacher split up the class for a group project, and the coach split up the team for a practice game. The researchers split up the volunteers into three groups.

verbs.correct: To notice and remember what you see
verbs.wrong: To start a new hobby or activity
verbs.why: Tourists stop to take in the view from the tower, and a new driver tries to take in every road sign. The volunteers looked at a set of images and tried to take in the details.

verbs.correct: To stay strong or good over time
verbs.wrong: To stop yourself from doing something
verbs.why: Cheap shoes rarely hold up through a whole winter, and a good friendship holds up even at a distance. Three days later, the researchers tested how well the memories had held up.

chunks.text: The two methods {{turned out}} to work in different ways. The study's lead author, a [[doctoral candidate]] in [[neurology]], {{pointed out}} that the nap let the brain [[recharge]]. The [[brain recordings]] showed that exercise made the brain use its [[resources]] more [[efficiently]], without adding [[fatigue]]. A hard ride might seem sure to {{wear down}} a tired body. Instead, the exercise group {{kept up with}} the nap group on the memory test. The senior author is a professor of [[physical therapy]] at McGill University.

verbs.correct: To be found to be true in the end
verbs.wrong: To refuse an offer or request
verbs.why: The cheap hotel turned out to be very clean, and the noisy neighbor turned out to be a kind person. The two methods turned out to work in different ways.

verbs.correct: To tell people an important fact
verbs.why: A guide points out the oldest building on the street, and a mechanic points out a worn tire before a long trip. The lead author pointed out that the nap let the brain recharge.

verbs.correct: To make someone weak and tired
verbs.wrong: To slowly stop having an effect
verbs.why: A long illness can wear down even a strong person, and months of night shifts wear down a nurse. A hard ride might seem sure to wear down a tired body.

verbs.correct: To do as well as someone else
verbs.why: A young runner can keep up with the adults in a short race, and a new student worked hard to keep up with the class. The exercise group kept up with the nap group on the memory test.

chunks.text: The findings matter for anyone who cannot {{catch up on}} sleep [[right away]]. Nurses, new parents, students and [[shift workers]] often {{go without}} a full night in bed. A short ride on a bike may help them {{bounce back}} until a real rest is possible. The study looked only at healthy young adults after a single [[sleepless]] night. Even so, moving your body for 20 minutes beats doing nothing at all.

verbs.correct: To do something you missed earlier
verbs.wrong: To become popular with many people
verbs.why: Students catch up on homework after a sick day, and travelers catch up on emails at the airport. Many people cannot catch up on sleep right away after a bad night.

verbs.correct: To live without something you need
verbs.why: Campers sometimes go without a hot shower for a week, and a busy family may go without dinner together. Nurses and shift workers often go without a full night in bed.

verbs.correct: To feel well again after a hard time
verbs.wrong: To make someone remember the past
verbs.why: A child bounces back quickly from a cold, and an athlete can bounce back after a painful loss. A short bike ride may help tired workers bounce back until real rest is possible.

mainIdea.s: Researchers kept 54 young adults awake for 30 hours. A short workout or a 90-minute nap then improved their memory by about 22 percent.
mainIdea.why: Both the exercise group and the nap group scored about 22 percent better than the group that did neither.

mainIdea.s: Researchers kept 54 young adults awake for 30 hours. A 90-minute nap improved their memory, but a short workout only made them more tired.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the workout helped memory just as much as the nap, and the brain recordings showed it did not add fatigue.

mainIdea.s: Researchers asked 54 young adults to sleep for 30 hours. Those who slept the longest remembered far more of the images three days later.
mainIdea.why: The volunteers were kept awake for 30 hours, not asleep, and the study compared a nap, a workout and doing nothing.

tf.s: Fifty-four healthy young adults took part in the experiment.
tf.why: They stayed up for 30 hours straight while researchers supervised them in a laboratory.

tf.s: The volunteers were split up into two groups after the long night.
tf.why: There were three groups: one cycled for 20 minutes, one took a 90-minute nap, and one did neither.

tf.s: The memory test came three days after the volunteers looked at the images.
tf.why: Everyone tried to take in the images right after the workout or the nap, and the researchers tested those memories three days later.

tf.s: The nap group scored far better than the exercise group on the memory test.
tf.why: The exercise group kept up with the nap group, and both scored about 22 percent better than the group that did neither.

tf.s: Exercise helped the tired brain without adding fatigue.
tf.why: Brain recordings showed the brain using its resources more efficiently, so the ride did not wear down the volunteers further.

tf.s: The nap made the brain use its resources more efficiently.
tf.why: It turned out that the nap let the brain recharge, while exercise was the method that made the brain work more efficiently.
